messages.subject: Duty cycles
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I am analyzing a dataset of 54 satellite tracked  Turkey Vultures, there are four different duty cycles (1 fix/3 hours, 1 fix/hour between 05:00 to 10:00, 1 fix/hour between 05:00 to 22:00, 1 fix/hour). I was recommended to standardize the sampling regime to  the longest on all the dataset.

Does someone knows if there is any resulting bias using different duty cycles to estimate AKDE of different individuals in the same population?

Thanks in advance. All the best,

Adrian

messages.subject: Re: Duty cycles
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian,

There is no need to standardize with AKDE. (You actually loose a little bit of efficiency doing that.) This is the advantage of working in continuous time.

However, if the vultures have one movement behavior at a certain time of day and a different movement behavior at different time of day, then you probably want to segment the data and estimate separate ranges, such as a foraging range, which is probably what you are interested in.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: alternative error values for estimating UERE
messages.subject_clean: alternative error values for estimating UERE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christina,

Using the number of satellites is (by default) a fallback model if no DOP value is detected in the data. I have a formula that automatically converts the satellite count into an approximate DOP value.
You can test whether or not this model outperforms your DOP values by importing the calibration data with and without the DOP column. The DOP values are supposed to be better, but sometimes they are garbage.
You can test whether or not either one of those models outperforms the homoskedastic error model by importing the calibration data without any of those columns.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: inadequate error model, recommendations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I was wondering what your recommendations are when the error model just doesn't seem to capture the nature of the GPS data.

Based on stationary tests I've conducted, the UERE comparisons indicate that DOP & fix type are the best error metrics:

                                    ΔAICc      Z[red]²

DOPandType              0.000        6.195841

TTF                             568.283    9.492835

DOP                           1659.623  19.525648

nSats                          2300.477  22.411890

all.error.values            3214.906  31.531827

But, my tests also indicate that the UERE estimates differ in areas of varying topography (I tested in three classes of low, med, high GPS interference). I'm not sure exactly how I could implement a topography-dependent UERE when the true location of the points is unknown.

If I ignore topography and just apply the UERE fit based on all stationary tests regardless of topographic class to data collected from my study animals (bighorn sheep), then I end up with outlier plots that look like this:

I picked 4 individuals in a particularly problematic area with high proportion of rugged terrain to highlight the extreme errors that I get. I think a heavy-tailed distribution would be best, but because ctmm doesn't currently handle this case, I was wondering what your recommendations are in this situation. I can implement approaches to flag and remove extreme points prior to model fitting (which on average is 1.8% of data per individual), but wondered if you had other ideas that didn't involve excluding data.

Thanks in advance for any suggestions you have

Christina

messages.subject: Re: inadequate error model, recommendations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christina,

Looking at the models you considered:
I am finding that a reduced Z^2 of a good GPS model seems to be 2-3, and 6 is is not very good. Yes, that looks like a heavy tailed error distribution with no clear cutoff between normative data and outliers, which is not supposed to happen with performant HDOP values.
Your top 2 models are DOP*Fix_Type and then TTF, but I didn't see DOP*Fix_Type*TTF. I would definitely consider that as well.
If (2.) doesn't fix the issue, then I would suspect multi-pathing (reflections) from topography, though that isn't supposed to happen in newer GPS modules.

It is true that you don't know exactly the topography of the true location, and so if that changes substantially within the scale of error, then its bad to estimate it with the topography of the estimated location. But the more exact inference is a nonlinear state estimation problem and is pretty challenging. Over what scale does your topography change enough to produce a large change in the UERE?

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Here's a more thorough comparison, which shows some improvement by using DOP with TTF:
                               ΔAICc          Z[red]²
DOP*TTF               0.0000         4.729551
DOP*FixType         413.0656      6.195841
TTF                        981.3487      9.492835
Type                       1304.9503   11.350043
DOP                       2072.6885   19.525648
nSats                      2713.5426   22.411890
DOP*FixType*TTF 3627.9715   31.531827
all.error.metrics      3627.9715   31.531827

If I estimate unique UERE's by topography class, it becomes the top model:
                                         ΔAICc          Z[red]²
DOPxTTF.TopoClass       0.0000         3.813689
DOPxTTF                        129.7971      4.729551
DOPxType                       542.8627     6.195841
TTF                                  1111.1457    9.492835
Type                                 1434.7473   11.350043
DOP                                 2202.4856   19.525648
nSats                               2843.3397    22.411890
DOPxTypexTTF               3757.7685    31.531827
all.error.metrics                3757.7685    31.531827

After applying the DOPxTTF error model to animal data (without considering topography), there is still the same pattern in the outlie plot - no clear cutoff point between the bulk of the data and outliers. I've fit the model without removing any outliers and the predicted path (shown in yellow) seems to do a pretty good job at avoiding those extreme spikes outside of the mountain range/bighorn habitat (I flagged bad points using different algorithms/approaches and show them in red, black, or orange; fix locations shown in white are assumed "good" quality).

We're using a modern GPS collar, but the company set the time to fix window to 70 seconds (to save battery life I think), with no way for the user to adjust this. We've contacted the company to adjust the setting to 180s TTF on some of our test collars and it substantially reduced the error, but collars were already deployed on animals at the 70s TTF, and can only be changed when in-hand. Ugh!

Unfortunately, the topography influence is pretty fine-scale - test locations 150 - 200m apart had different UERE estimates.
At the regional scale, there are differences in how predominant those topography classes are, so particular populations will have data with more error than others because there's more habitat prone to bad fixes available.

Just to give you an idea of what I'm hoping to achieve long-term - I'm interested in estimating each animal's actual movement path or occurrence distribution (not homerange) in order to assess movement patterns relative to highway barriers (which sections of highway are approached more often and when by bighorn), and to identify habitat conditions associated with movement paths that cross between mountain ranges. Perhaps the error model applied above does a good enough job?

Thanks again for your thoughts on this!

Christina

messages.subject: Re: Data cleaning best practices
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vickie,

Sorry for the delay, I had to have my appendix removed.

 Obvious outliers are generally good to remove, unless they have an appropriately large DOP values and you are sparse on data.
I'm not sure where 'amt' fits in here, but I'm not super familiar with the package.
When you have outliers, its a good idea to figure out if there is some proxy/covariate associated with them when DOP value doesn't (DOP value is supposed to). I do this by importing the data with keep=TRUE, running uere.fit, uere<-, residuals, and then plotting the square residuals against different columns/covariates. I've seen cases where 3D/2D fixes needed to be broken into two different location classes, because otherwise the 2D fixes looked like outliers (DOP value is supposed to account for this). I've seen cases where timed-out fixes needed to be broken into two different location classes, because otherwise the timed-out fixes looked like outliers (again, DOP value is supposed to account for this). The only thing I recall about your data from AniMove was that you had outliers corresponding with location fixes that were at higher than programed sampling rates (2 minutes versus 1 hour or something). If you can figure out something that gives a larger variance in the errors, then you can either introduce a new location class and try to model that variance or filter out those locations. You might use the reduced Z^2 statistic to guide that decision.
Yes, that's what the outlie function is for.
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: inadequate error model, recommendations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christina,

Sorry for the delay, I had to have my appendix removed.

I think I see one issue with your model comparison: DOP*TTF and DOP*FixType are both nested inside DOP*FixType*TTF, so I wouldn't expect AICc to be worse by more than ~2, when compared to the best of DOP*TTF and DOP*FixType . In fact, (biased) AIC can only be worse by at-most 2 in cases like this. I would try to make sure the DOP*FixType*TTF model is correctly specified. I suspect it is not.

Best,
Chris
